stories.title: Batavian woman
stories.caption: Labeled 'a mestiza,' this image depicts a woman of mixed background in Batavia/Jakarta, wearing a wrapped patterned textile for a skirt, a white upper garment, and loose jacket.
stories.creator: Anonymous copy after Andries Beeckman

annotations.text: These long triangles at the border of her wrapped skirt are typical of printed and painted textiles made for the Javanese market.
These meandering floral designs were desirable across the global market for chintz.
The primary colors of chintz are the underlying white fabric, red (chay or madder), blue (indigo), with black/brown linework. Other dyes, like yellow (turmeric) were more fleeting.
This image of a mixed-race woman (titled 'mestiza') was painted by a follower of Andries Beeckman ca. 1675–1725.

annotations.text: Approximate pattern repeat. This length of cloth was handpainted, so the pattern repeats are slightly different in proportion and detail.

The primary colors of chintz are the underlying white fabric, red (chay or madder), blue (indigo), with black/brown linework. Here, layered dyes create a range of hues of reds, purples, and blue-greens.
This chintz was made ca. 1750 in India by an unknown artist.

annotations.text: Bundles of gifts, wrapped in white cloth, rest in front of the vice king, carried by Dutchmen up the aisle.

annotations.text: The name "guinees stuff" here refers to one of many types of blue-and-white cloth shipped to the western coast of Africa.

Blue with thin horizontal and vertical stripes, this sample represents a type of patterning sometimes seen in guinea cloth. Corroots--a type of guinea cloth--and bejutapauts (samples below) more closely resemble the patterning in the skirt of Eckhout's painting of an African woman.

stories.caption: This image shows a mardijker wearing striped pants, which may have been made from nickanees. He stands next to his wife, who holds a child.
stories.creator: after Johan Nieuhof

annotations.text: This image, titled “A Mardijker and his Wife” is from Johan Nieuhof's Zee- en Lant-Reise door verscheide Gewesten van Oostindien (Amsterdam, 1682) . The term “mardijker”—derived from the Portuguese term mardicas (“free people”)—was used to describe formerly enslaved people, or the descendants of the former enslaved.
The marijker picture by Nieuhof wears a striped doublet and pants strikingly similar in pattern to nickanees , which circulated on WIC and VOC ships in Asia and Africa .

stories.title: Portrait of a Kongo Ambassador to Recife, Brazil
stories.caption: Because of his status as a member of the Kongo Christian elite, the man’s attire shows both local and foreign elements of attire. His heavy dark blue cloak – perhaps made out of wool – in combination with the white fabric wrapped around his waist and held in place by a blue and white checkered textile indicate his status. Perhaps his red sash is a perpetuaan?
stories.creator: Albert Eckhout (1610–1665)
stories.credit: Jagiellonian Library, Krakow, Libri Picturati A 34

stories.title: Muslim galley slaves carrying a sail
stories.caption: Five men carry a rolled sail on their shoulders, presumably from one of the ships in the background at right, to shore. Is the sail being moved to shore for repairs, or is this a damaged or old sail that will be put to new use? The galley slaves, whose status is indicated by ankle shackles, have a uniform appearance with similar moustaches and shaved heads. Their clothing is also similar in appearance, long-sleeved tunics hanging loose over short breeches, which could also be made from sail cloth.
stories.creator: M. Schaep after Cornelis de Wael

annotations.text: These figures carry a rolled sail, made from sail cloth.

stories.title: Pieter de Marees, Marketplace in Cabo Corso, Description and Historical Account of the Gold Coast of Guinea, 1602
stories.caption: In this well-known image from De Marees’s text, a merchant measures linen, labeled here with an L. The caption below reads: “Holland Linen, which [they] have brought ashore from the ship lying opposite their quarter, is measured out in fathoms and remeasured.” In a later section he notes that after measuring out 2 fathoms of linens, “they cut the cloth into strips which are only about the width of one hand and use these instead of girdles around their bodies. They sell cloth in this form among themselves and it is not traded or distributed among them in any other measurements.”
stories.creator: Theodore de Bry, after anonymous.

annotations.text: The caption below this merchant (labeled with an “L”) reads: “Holland Linen, which [they] have brought ashore from the ship lying opposite their quarter, is measured out in fathoms and remeasured.” Although not a slaaplaken, this image and the accompanying text suggests there was a strong market for linen in the region.
This image, titled "Marketplace in Cabo Corso," was published in Pieter de Marees's 1602 Description of the Gold Coast of Guinea (Amsterdam, 1602).

gallery.title: Esaias Boursse, Interior with Woman Cooking, 1656. Wallace Collection, London.
gallery.caption: Europeans compared the blue-and-white textiles they reported to have seen in Africa as reminiscent of “feather bed tykes,” perhaps similar to what Boursse pictured in the background of his painting. The white sheets that hang over the frame of the bed are likely slaaplakens (bedsheets), which were traded in large numbers on the west coast of Africa.
